text: We had barely digested the news of the sale of Merrill Lynch and the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers, and suddenly the Wall Street soap opera was all about AIG. AIG stock fell by more than half today. Since the year began, it's down 90 percent. American International Group is the giant of the insurance business, and it is evidently seeking a giant loan or some assistance from the Federal Reserve to stave off disaster. AIG's dilemma raises questions. Is a company with a trillion dollars of assets too big to fail? How does a company that big get into that much trouble? And what exactly does AIG do? Well, for answers to those questions, starting with the first, we've called on Diane Brady, senior writer at Business Week. Diane, AIG in a nutshell.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Writer, Business Week)
text: Well, as you said, it is one of the largest insurers on the planet, never mind the U.S. And it's not just in general insurance, it's in life insurance, retirement services, asset management, and financial services which of course is an area that got it into trouble.
Yeah. The company's reported to be looking for a loan of 30 to 40 billion dollars, a bridge loan. What went so wrong at AIG that they should need a loan that big?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Writer, Business Week)
text: Well, they've had a couple of things go wrong. One is the fact that they've had this credit derivative portfolio that's been tied to subprime-backed securities. Obviously that's been a tough area, and those losses basically have risen steadily as the subprime mortgage crisis has worsened. But AIG's also had its own investment portfolio where they were involved in subprime, and they have a mortgage insurance unit. So they've been hit on a number of fronts. But one other problem for AIG, I think, is that there's been rampant short-selling of the stock. So that kept driving the stock down, and at the same time that the company was running out of cash.

Well, one of the questions raised by AIG's problem is, does it qualify as the kind of entity, like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, that is simply too big for the U.S. government to allow to fail? Or is it in the same category as Lehman Brothers: big, fabled, but basically on its own?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Writer, Business Week)
text: I think that's an excellent question, because you could ask the same of the car companies. Obviously, GM has found out that they are not going to be as eligible for federal assistance as some people thought. I think there's a couple of things here. One, the Federal Reserve obviously does not regulate AIG. Insurance is a state matter. But in the press conference today, Governor Patterson said that the insurance commissioner has talked to federal regulators about trying to help AIG get the resources it needs.
This is David Patterson...

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Writer, Business Week)
text: David Patterson.
The governor of New York state, yeah.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Writer, Business Week)
text: And they do not want this company to fail. It's in too many areas, it's too big, and the ripple effects would just be too profound.
Well, let's say there is no federal loan. What else might there be in the way of saving AIG?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Writer, Business Week)
text: Well, it's hard. I mean, at one point, AIG probably could've tapped into some of the sovereign wealth funds, which is countries, for example, the Middle East which have a lot of capital right now and could be investing. But the immediate thing right now is they've got 20 billion dollars they can tap from their own units. Beyond that, the question is, where are they going to get the money in this market? I can't see many places they can get it other than the Fed, in part because everybody else is strained on their balance sheet as well. And a lot of the people like the sovereign wealth funds are sitting on the sidelines just witnessing the sheer extent of carnage right now on Wall Street. They're starting to wonder about the future of Wall Street itself, what the regulatory environment's going to be. So AIG's in a very delicate position. It does not have a lot of places to turn.
Diane Brady, thanks a lot for talking with us.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Writer, Business Week)
text: Thank you.
Diane Brady, senior writer at Business Week.
Diane Brady is a senior editor at Business Week, and she joins us from our New York bureau. She's here to help us make sense of the government's plans for AIG. Welcome back to the program.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Nice to be here. Thanks.
Diane, this is widely described as a bailout. Is that actually the right term?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Technically, it's a loan. But in essence, it is a bailout because this is a company that could have gone bankrupt. The government does want to characterize it as a loan. It's 85 billion dollars. It's loan shark rates in some respects, double digits that AIG has to pay back. But in essence, the question is taxpayers could still be on the hook, and they now essentially own 80 percent of this company.
What happens if they don't pay that back at those, as you say, loan shark rates?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Well, in essence AIG is going to be trying to sell off its assets as quickly as possible, but try to get the best price. The issue right now is that there just is not a lot of money in the markets. You look at the fact that the government did say no to AIG. Then it had to come back and say yes. Why? What happened in that interim is they went to Wall Street. Wall Street didn't have the cash. Investors don't have faith at the moment. There's nowhere else to get the cash. So, people are hoping it's aspirational, that AIG is able to pay this back. But they have a lot of debt. They have a lot of obligations on their books. If the whole market blows up, somebody's going to be on the hook for it. And now the biggest owner of this company essentially is the government and the taxpayers.
But the government doesn't actually own AIG. They have a 79.9 percent equity stake.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Exactly.
Exactly what does that mean? What kind of terms can they dictate?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: They have warrants. They do - they are able to dictate. And you see that in the fact that the CEO was immediately replaced with somebody that, of course, Paulson and Bernanke picked, the former Allstate CEO. So I think essentially the government is now calling the shots. What they're trying to do here is contain the crisis. That's the big issue. What they don't want is to see the problems at AIG cascade. So the people who are the frontline sufferers in this are the shareholders. Essentially, the value for them has been wiped out by this move.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: The angriest person today you'll find is Hank Greenberg, the former chairman. He was the largest single individual shareholder. He wanted a loan to this company, short-term capital. Instead what they did was essentially, in his eyes, nationalize it, because what they said is, OK, fine, we'll lend to you, but we're going to essentially call the shots at this point.
Now, tell me about Edward Liddy. Who is he, and what exactly is his charge?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Well, he is the former Allstate CEO. He's on the board of Boeing. He knows a lot about the domestic property casualty business. Is he somebody you would pick to run AIG as an entity that stays together? No. Because it's a huge financial services giant. It's global. It's in 130 countries. What he is going to be charged with doing is trying to find the highest bidders for AIG's assets. Some of those bidders may be people who've already been circling, such as Hank Greenberg, the former chairman. But what he's trying to do is make sure that there is the orderly disposal of assets so that the government gets its money back as quickly as possible.
So the Federal Reserve said it wanted to avoid a disorderly failure. This is something like the - it seems that they're trying instead to oversee a more controlled dismantling?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Exactly. And one thing that people - I think has been out there that's a little misunderstood about AIG, this is not a case that this company is just so big, and we all hold policies, and so wouldn't it be terrible if AIG fails? The issue is that they are the ones that have backed a lot of these mortgage-backed securities. As this market has been spiraling, if AIG backs out of the picture, then all of a sudden there's a domino effect, and everybody else starts to fall. That's the concern here, is that all the counter parties, all the people that have done business with AIG, if this company had gone under would suddenly have to face the reality of their own assets, and we could see a lot more failures. At this point, the economy is so weak they don't want that to happen.
Diane, very, very quickly, because I have to let you go. Does that mean the government is on the hook for those insurance policies?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: The government is on the hook for the success of the sale of AIG at this point. They - the shareholders are essentially out of the picture. The people who are going to have to make sure this works are the U.S. taxpayers.
That's Diane Brady, senior editor at Business Week. Diane, thank you very much.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Thank you.

Even by the standards of undercapitalized banks with TARP funds and bankrupt auto companies and nominally independent government-sponsored mortgage entities, the relationship of AIG to the federal government is stunning. The insurance giant got a $180 billion bailout from the government. It paid out bonuses earlier this year that infuriated many. On the other hand, it's now losing senior management because of a $500,000 compensation cap. And the New York Federal Reserve has evidently told AIG not to discuss payments that were made with federal bailout funds to its own trading partners, which is generally taken to mean to Goldman Sachs.
Diane Brady, senior editor at Business Week, tells us that she is immersed in all things AIG these days. So, welcome to the program to share in your immersion with us.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Thanks. Nice to be here.
And let's start with that last controversy. What is it that some members of Congress want to know about AIG that the New York Fed has told them not to disclose?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Well, what they want to know now is whether Treasury Secretary Tim Geithner was involved in these emails to AIG that was essentially pressuring them to withhold information on payments that it made to the banks.
He at that time was...

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: He was the president of the New York Fed. And I think what has subsequently made the public so angry is this is a company that was on the precipice of disaster, was going to go the way of Lehman and basically these contracts, which were worth very little, the banks were getting a hundred cents on the dollar.
Banks insured their investments with AIG, and AIG, even as it was bust and had only federal funds to go on, was paying off a hundred cents on the dollar.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Yes. AIG basically was doing these credit default swaps, which is in essence a form of insurance policy on these collateralized debt obligations, which is the bundling of all these toxic mortgages. But one other thing that has made people angry - and I know Goldman Sachs has been so vilified in the past year - is Goldman Sachs, we've since discovered, created and sold these collateralized debt obligations and then it sold them short, which basically means they were pressuring the credit agencies to say they were solid bets even as the firm was betting against them. But the heart of the matter is the public money was being used to pay a hundred cents on the dollar on contracts that were in no way worth that much.
Because Goldman Sachs was betting against these securities by going to AIG and insuring with them.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Exactly.
Was AIG being stood up, in fact, as a conduit of federal funds passing through it to those other banks?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Exactly. And I think especially when you see Goldman Sachs coming out and paying what some people have deemed to be egregious bonuses, but they've had a banner year and one reason they've had a banner year is in part because they've benefited from situations like AIG where, had the company gone under, they would have had to fight for their money. Instead, they walked away with a hundred cents on the dollar of every dollar that they put in.

Now AIG, like a lot of other companies that received bailout funds, has said we don't want to see caps on compensation because we'll lose talent. And, in fact, their general counsel, the head of HR as well at AIG, is leaving because she says she's not getting enough.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: I think it's a complex issue. Yes, there are caps. I think there have to be caps right now in part to assuage Washington and the public, who do not want to see both millions in payout and millions in salary. I think AIG also has the - the big issue, frankly, is that its brand is very tarnished and its future is very uncertain. And if you're, let's say, CEO material or certainly senior executive material, you would think twice about going to AIG. So they're going to have trouble. They have had trouble recruiting people, but it's especially hard to recruit people when you can't pay marketplace dollars, and frankly for a general counsel, they tend to make more than 500,000 a year.
Hmm. Well, what's the future for this company? I mean, is it clear that it will actually survive for a few more years or is this the wind-down of AIG?

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: I think that's a very good question and people aren't quite sure. I mean, even the stock has been very skittish. But basically they're looking to sell off a lot of assets. They're having trouble retaining their people. The brand - where possible, they've dropped the name. And I think a lot of people are very skittish about the future and at the very least they think that the government support is going to continue for quite sometime.
Diane Brady, senior editor at Business Week, thanks a lot for talking with us.

speaker_label: Ms. DIANE BRADY (Senior Editor, Business Week)
text: Thank you.
